Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
When will the war in Iran end? American officials claim that the answer is soon. “I think the war is going to end immediately after the [November] election,” declared U.S. President Donald Trump in September. “They can’t hold out any longer.” Iranian leaders agree that the war’s conclusion is near. Tehran has “brought the most heavily armed army in the history of the world to its knees,” proclaimed Ahmad Vahidi, the commander in chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, in August. Many outside analysts think that the conflict will drag on for longer and end with negotiations rather than with a clear winner. But generally, there is a sense that the fighting will soon be resolved, one way or another.
Such thinking is understandable. All wars eventually end, and after months of rising energy prices, the world is especially eager for this one to stop. Yet the unsettling reality is that the conflict is nowhere near over. The war’s two principal belligerents cannot achieve their desired goals, yet they both feel they are accomplishing enough to make continued fighting through a mix of military and economic tools worth it. The United States cannot topple the Iranian regime, get it to give up its missile program, force it to abandon its nuclear program, or make it stop supporting its regional partners. But Washington can keep degrading Iran’s military and constricting its economy. Iran cannot evict the world’s only superpower from the Middle East. Yet it can keep damaging U.S. regional bases, bombing the United States’ regional allies, and disrupting international commerce.
Critically, both states have the resources needed to fight indefinitely—and both believe they have no choice but to use them. They think that if their side lets up, the other will press on until it has either humiliated them or achieved its main objectives. They carry out periodic talks, but there is no mutual trust. In fact, they suspect that their enemy will simply use a cease-fire to regroup and resupply before attacking again. The Iranian government fears that relinquishing leverage, whether over Hormuz, its missile arsenal, or the nuclear program, would leave it exposed to pressure later. Washington, for its part, worries that sweeping sanctions relief would provide Tehran with the resources and time it needs to reconstitute its capabilities. Israel, meanwhile, fears that restraint today would only create a stronger Iran tomorrow. The steps required to escape the war look dangerous precisely because they require each side to temporarily make itself more vulnerable.
The war, then, will carry on as it has. There will not be a comprehensive resolution. There will be no lasting peace deal. But because the status quo is sustainable for each side, and because the parties lack the power to seize the upper hand, there will be no dramatic escalation, either. Tehran and Washington won’t be defeated. Yet no one will win.
For the United States, the war was not supposed to go like this. When it joined Israel in striking the Islamic Republic on February 28, Washington thought that it would quickly prevail. The two countries, after all, had buried or destroyed most of Iran’s nuclear facilities and blown up many of its missile sites in June 2025. Israel had killed scores of senior Iranian scientists and more than two dozen military leaders, and it had decimated Hezbollah in Lebanon. Syrian President Bashar al-Assad—a longtime Iranian ally—had lost power, and massive protests had just rocked the Iranian government itself. The U.S. military and the Israel Defense Forces enjoyed what seemed like uncontested access to Iranian airspace. The regime, in other words, appeared to be on the precipice.
In the conflict’s opening days, Israel and the United States killed Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and many of the country’s top military commanders. But predictions that the Islamic Republic would collapse proved incorrect. The regime quickly replaced lost officials and set about striking back at its enemies, blowing up American jets, missile launchers, and radar systems on bases scattered throughout the Persian Gulf. It took control of the Strait of Hormuz and squeezed commercial flows through the waterway. And Iranian forces attacked civilian infrastructure across the Gulf region, making Washington’s regional partners pay for enabling the U.S.-Israeli assault.
American officials have downplayed these setbacks, promising that the Iranian regime is just one more strike or sanction away from being forced to make concessions. But it is extremely unlikely that Israel and Washington will force Tehran to compromise on anything significant. They have repeatedly tried to bomb the regime’s officials and military programs out of existence, only for Tehran to rapidly rebuild them. It is hard to see how future airstrikes can accomplish what past ones haven’t.
The United States, of course, has added a new dimension to its assault, piling on sanctions to accompany its blockade of Iran’s southern coast and periodic bombings. These measures have succeeded in further constricting Iran’s access to global markets, including its ability to import various wares and export key commodities such as oil. But this, too, is unlikely to persuade the regime. Overland routes and the Caspian Sea conspire against any attempt to hermetically seal Iran, even if the capacity of these passageways cannot compensate for the closing of naval routes and dwindling air links. China and Russia have provided a variety of goods and valuable military intelligence. The economic effect of the U.S. cutoffs is real, but the government will pass on the damage to its people by reducing subsidies rather than curbing spending on military and security services, which it needs to defend against external adversaries and internal dissent. The public must contend head-on with a collapsing currency and runaway inflation, and to ordinary Iranians, describing the present situation as sustainable would sound almost obscene. But what might be unsustainable for Iranian society can be perfectly sustainable for the state. The Islamic Republic does not need to protect Iran as a whole from economic deterioration. It must protect only the institutions and constituencies necessary for its own survival.
U.S. officials may hope that as Iran’s population becomes poorer, Tehran will have a change of heart. But Iranian leaders believe they are confronting an existential challenge, and in such circumstances, leaders are unlikely to regard any level of economic hardship as a clear breaking point. Plus, the regime has endured a worse situation without blinking, and for a longer time. From 1980 to 1988, the country fought a war with Iraq that killed hundreds of thousands of Iranians and left the state with hundreds of billions of dollars in damage. But even that was not enough to make Tehran quit. In fact, even after Iran expelled Iraqi forces from its territory, it invaded its adversary and spent six years trying to topple Iraqi President Saddam Hussein, despite continued domestic suffering. It took Iraqi battlefield advances, growing U.S. involvement in the Gulf, and a perception that the regional balance of power was moving sharply against Tehran to bring the conflict to a halt.
The United States, of course, has not played all its cards. It could put boots on the ground. But such operations would probably result in far more U.S. casualties and drive energy prices even higher. For these reasons, they are politically infeasible. Washington could launch airstrikes against major infrastructure targets, causing generational damage to Iran’s energy network, transportation and communications systems, and other facilities. But Tehran would retaliate in kind against American partners in the Gulf, also spiking energy costs.
Iran’s regime has celebrated its resilience in the face of U.S. attacks. But its prospects for defeating the United States look similarly grim. The country cannot easily increase the pressure because its economic distress narrows the margin for strategic recklessness. Iran’s leadership may believe it can survive prolonged hardship, yet another major confrontation with the United States would risk deeper damage amid an already strained social compact. Just as important, Iranian officials have little reason to believe that dramatic escalation would compel Washington to retreat; it could just as easily trigger a far more destructive response from an impulsive U.S. president. For now, Tehran is therefore likely to prefer imposing calibrated costs on the United States, preserving leverage, and testing American resolve without crossing a threshold that prompts intensive attacks.
And even if Tehran did dramatically escalate, the Islamic Republic is unlikely to triumph. Iran can weaken the United States’ regional footprint, and it has already forced the country to spend enormous sums—over $40 billion and counting—on the conflict. Yet the overall U.S. budget is in the trillions of dollars, and Washington has a large stockpile of less sophisticated bombs it could use to fight back as it runs low on advanced ones. It has lost troops, but only a tiny fraction of what it lost in Afghanistan and Iraq. And it can keep casualties relatively low because it can fight from a distance, lobbing missiles from outside Iranian territory.
At first, the fact that neither Tehran nor Washington can win outright might seem to bode well for peace. When countries realize that victory is unachievable, they sometimes settle. But both Iran and the United States have secondary aims, and they believe that continuing to fight will help achieve them. Washington, for example, thinks that occasional attacks will ensure that Tehran can never fully regenerate its military or develop nuclear weapons. It wants to strike Iran whenever the regime crosses a particular threshold, such as by rebuilding a particularly concerning weapons system or resuming nuclear enrichment. In so doing, the United States believes that it can keep Iran weak without assuming the political and military risks of attempting to transform it.
Iran, for its part, believes that continued fighting will help it establish the deterrence it has lost. It is mobilizing its regional partners, such as Iraqi militias and the Houthis in Yemen, to keep its adversaries under fire from multiple fronts. The regime has also become more willing to strike first. In July, for instance, it launched a missile attack on a base in Jordan that hosts U.S. military personnel, even though there was no American strike immediately preceding it. And, of course, it has sought to dominate the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian officials previously regarded shuttering the waterway as a measure of last resort, to be attempted only in extreme circumstances. They therefore waited until an all-out war erupted. But within a day, Tehran proved that it could control the strait by targeting ships with drones and missiles, giving it a new source of leverage.
Iran also seems to think that continued fighting will help it regain and perhaps expand the clout that had waned before the war, when it repeatedly failed to deter rivals and its regional partners lost influence. This explains why, when Israel and the United States hit Iran in February, it responded by immediately widening the battlefield to the entire Middle East—including Gulf countries that had spent recent years rebuilding relations with Tehran. In total, Iran has attacked over a dozen countries across the Middle East. It wants to persuade these states to pivot away from Washington by proving that partnering with the United States makes them vulnerable.
Washington’s and Tehran’s assessments might be right, or they might be wrong. But even if both stand to gain nothing from continued fighting—and even if both realize it—they will struggle to reach a resolution. Because Iranian officials believe that their American counterparts are bent on the destruction of the Islamic Republic, they do not think they can stop fighting even if they wanted to. Washington is not similarly fearful, but it still believes that it cannot afford to give in. In the eyes of U.S. officials, if the United States offers Iran the things it most wants—sweeping sanctions relief and recognition of the regime’s leverage over the Strait of Hormuz—it will have empowered its adversary and rewarded military coercion.
In theory, Iran and the United States could resolve these concerns via diplomacy. But in practice, neither trusts the other enough to make lasting tradeoffs. Consider, for instance, what happened to the memorandum of understanding the two sides signed in June in hopes of stopping the war. The deal was supposed to address both countries’ priorities by reopening the Strait of Hormuz and setting up negotiations over Tehran’s nuclear program in exchange for widespread sanctions relief and an end to attacks on Iran and its partners. But it quickly became clear that U.S. and Iranian officials did not agree on the details. Washington argued that the deal meant ships could again pass through the strait in whatever way they wanted, whereas Tehran argued that it could still dictate the manner of transit and impose fees. It thus fired on ships traveling through the waterway along Oman’s coastline rather than along its own, infuriating U.S. officials. Iran, meanwhile, accused Washington of violating the deal by not immediately releasing the country’s frozen assets and not stopping Israel from striking Hezbollah. Both sides concluded that the other was acting in bad faith, and the conflict resumed.
That failure doesn’t mean Tehran and Washington will not negotiate. They will likely maintain a dialogue, and they may periodically pause the conflict to regroup. But diplomacy and war can happen simultaneously. In the 1950s, for example, North Korea and the United States engaged diplomatically for years before reaching a durable cease-fire. As long as Tehran and Washington remain capable of and committed to hurting each other, the war won’t end no matter how much they talk.
The war against Iran may have settled into a stasis. But the conflict is transforming both the Islamic Republic and the surrounding region. Traditionally, Iran has been a complex autocracy, with a political order that mixes clerical authority, elected institutions, powerful security and military agencies, competing patronage networks, and a vibrant society. But the death of Khamenei eliminated the regime’s paramount figure, disturbing the existing balance, and the war is systematically privileging the parts of the state responsible for survival over everything else. Permanent conflict will only further elevate Iranians in uniform over Iranians in suits—and perhaps even over Iranians in clerical garb. The Islamic Republic’s already withered participatory institutions will keep fading, and the power of its military and security elites will be shrouded by a thinning theocratic cloak.
That does not mean the nonarmed parts of the country’s traditional power structure will be unable to exercise influence. Civilian politicians may still debate whether Iran should try to negotiate and how much economic pain the country can tolerate. But their ideas will be completely at the mercy of the armed elite, who prioritize restoring deterrence and preserving enough offensive capability to hurt Iran’s adversaries. The country is not going to eliminate its civilian institutions, but more and more areas of life are being defined as security issues—telecommunications, foreign investment, universities, the media, economic policy—and are thus coming under the security establishment’s command. The regime’s religious ethos will continue. But a clerical establishment that once cultivated the military to buttress its rule may end up being subordinate to it.
The Arab Gulf states, meanwhile, are reworking their security doctrines. Some of their thinking will please Iran: after decades of trying to keep Washington involved in the region out of fear that a U.S. withdrawal would leave them vulnerable, the Gulf states have concluded that close ties with the United States make them targets. But the Gulf is unlikely to evict Washington. For all its shortcomings, the United States is still the only outside country providing them with some measure of military support, and their distrust of Iran has deepened since the war began. In fact, some Gulf states have even retaliated against the Islamic Republic.
Instead, these countries are likely to hedge. They will create stronger diplomatic and economic linkages to Iran in hopes of persuading it to stop striking them. But they will retain security and economic ties with Washington. At the same time, they will start trying to develop stronger domestic missile defenses, harden their infrastructure, establish alternative energy export routes, and build larger strategic reserves of oil, gas, and arms. The region may also try to use its ties to both Iran and the United States to mediate the conflict.
Wars are chaotic by definition, and it is possible that a future attack or event could disrupt the current equilibrium. As both countries become more comfortable with the status quo, they might grow overly confident in their defenses and decide to escalate. Washington, for example, could be tempted to force the regime to buckle with a more fearsome military assault—leading Iran to cause greater market turmoil and damage to the Gulf. If an Iranian missile kills large numbers of Americans or an Iranian attack shuts down critical Gulf infrastructure, the United States might opt to finally use ground forces or destroy Iran’s electric grid, putting the regime in peril. Tehran could also be wrong to think that it can continue to inflict enormous pain on its people. Cascading goods shortages could prompt renewed mass unrest and elite defections, making it harder for the regime to keep fighting the United States while still maintaining power. An apparently manageable deterioration might become something much more dangerous: a declining capacity to govern, not merely a dwindling capacity to fight.
But for now, the war seems sustainable. Washington has not achieved any of its stated objectives, and it has burned through expensive munitions. Yet the United States can still afford to battle, and it believes that the costs of giving in exceed the costs of continuing. Iranian society is facing years of impoverishment and insecurity. Yet the Islamic Republic itself is stable, and it does not think it can afford to make meaningful concessions.
Such is the paradox of this conflict. Both sides have emerged weaker. Neither can win. But they fight on regardless, because they find the alternatives to be completely unpalatable.
ALI VAEZ is Deputy Program Director for the Middle East and North Africa at the International Crisis Group.
articles.summary: Why America and Iran fight on without victory.

articles.title: Rewiring the Arsenal of Democracy
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
Dan Driscoll was Secretary of the Army from 2025 to 2026.
The post–Cold War international order slowly withered for decades, but it reached a clear inflection point on June 1, 2025. On that day, Ukraine deployed less than a million dollars’ worth of hobby-shop technology to destroy Russian strategic bombers worth billions. Russia’s exquisite air defenses and geographic depth made no difference, and images of burning Russian bombers finally settled the debate as to whether drones are a tactical aberration or a tectonic shift in geopolitical power. Operation Spider’s Web, as the Ukrainian operation was named, codified the rules of the new era: bespoke platforms are luxury items and “mass”—the ability to employ more weapons faster and for a longer period—is essential.
This radical change necessitates continued reform in the United States’ defense ecosystem. As many have noted, the technological advances of private commercial firms are outpacing those made by traditional defense industries, artificial intelligence is accelerating innovation, and the wide diffusion of technology is blurring the capabilities of state and nonstate actors. Less appreciated, however, is how this new era is also changing the currencies of international statecraft. By transforming the application of violence and expanding warfare from limited conflicts to existential risks, this inflection point requires a new way of thinking about and constructing alliances.
Since the end of World War II, the United States’ greatest deterrence factor has been unified alliances whose combined military might is preeminent. But this allied might is only as dominant as the sum of the parts. As the war in Ukraine and conflict in the Middle East have demonstrated, many large militaries are not prepared for the current era of mass-produced precision strikes and interceptions. Defense industries are still structured around expensive, exquisite, and proprietary military platforms.
The United States’ strength depends on strong alliances, with a shared defense industrial base that can aggregate capabilities for a new era of warfare. To get there, Washington must encourage a free-market, international defense ecosystem defined by open architecture and industrial, software, and hardware compatibility. The United States’ greatest deterrent, the foundation of its diplomatic clout, and the primary factor in its ability to win on the modern battlefield this next century will be its collective allied industrial capacity and military interoperability. If it fails to secure such a strategy of compatibility, other state and nonstate actors will be meaningfully more likely to take escalatory actions.
Conceptually, the idea of interoperability and collective defense innovation is well trodden. But practically, it has never come to fruition at scale. The global defense architecture is still oriented toward a Cold War–era industrial model. This model generally involves U.S. defense companies creating small batches of exquisite equipment that is operated with proprietary, siloed software. Allies would purchase this equipment and combine it with their own nation’s military offerings, wherever possible. Most companies were incentivized to create defensive moats around their products once they were sold to prevent competition from replacing them.
All this unfolded at a time of relative global peace, so the special interest decision-making model amplified the entrenchment of these companies and created a mosaic of military platforms and systems. The United States and its allies recognized that the digital revolution of the past 20 years would require more compatibility, but they deferred to the momentum of their acquisition processes and chose to only tinker on the margins rather than embark on fundamental change.
This complacency led to the level of unpreparedness that U.S. President Donald Trump inherited last year. The U.S.-led defense architecture had successfully deterred large-scale conflict for decades, but the U.S. Army in 2025 looked shockingly similar to that of 1975. Because the incentive was to maintain the status quo rather than steer the future of warfare, the U.S. defense industry had devolved into an oligopoly. A handful of so-called prime contractors developed exquisite platforms with built-in firewalls and produced them in custom-built factories. Meanwhile, decades of government statutes and policies, along with poor acquisition incentives, optimized for job distribution over efficacy and ultimately encouraged contractors to make platforms that are expensive and slow to replace—in other words, the antithesis of affordable mass. Overregulation also paralyzed foreign military sales, and procedural and financial barriers to entry locked out small and medium-sized companies.
With all these same dynamics at play in other countries, U.S. allies each suffered from their own isolated oligopolies. The allied industrial base—and thus Washington’s ability to fight as a coalition—atrophied.
Contrast this dynamic with private technology companies, which are perpetually at war for their survival. Over the same period, these companies have made advances that have driven humanity into the future. They race toward minimally viable products, tighter innovation cycles, and ever-evolving and improving offerings. And they pursue open data architectures to ensure their products meet industry standards to exchange data across the Internet. A smartphone that cannot exchange data, after all, is simply an expensive paperweight.
The stark divide between open and closed systems is something I witnessed firsthand earlier this year. At Grafenwoehr Training Area in Germany, I watched allied forces and Ukrainian forces test counterdrone capabilities in a combat scenario. The allied soldiers performed well in a scenario that mimicked previous conflicts with limited air threats, but their systems were not designed for the large drone swarms of modern combat. As the air threats were layered into the exercise, I watched an allied air defender swivel from one screen to the next, manually transferring data from one proprietary system to another. The kill chain—the sequence of steps between identifying a target and destroying it—was only as fast and accurate as his keystrokes.
The Ukrainian soldiers, by contrast, were able to monitor threats and activate offensive and defensive capabilities from one system, on one screen, and with just a few keystrokes. Faced with the existential risk of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, the Ukrainians have embraced open-source data standards and AI-enabled kill chains. The result is seamless data transfer fused onto a single user interface. It was amazing to see what is possible when all elements of the system are knit together from the factory floor to the foxhole. I also saw clearly the limit of allied military power: isolated capabilities that cannot withstand the intensity of today’s battlefields.
When domestic defense industries create bespoke, proprietary software, it results in inconsistent technical specifications. Systems physically cannot share data across platforms, and each country’s exquisite capabilities resemble a walled garden—impressive on their own but useless to anyone on the other side of the wall. This degrades combat effectiveness since modern command and control requires split-second detection and engagement.
Countering future threats is beyond human cognitive capacity—only AI can manage the speed and volume of data, which is why compatibility is the linchpin of modern military strategy. The only way to achieve this is to break down the walls and abandon top-down military standardization. Washington and its allies must embrace private-industry best practices that enforce compatibility from inception, lower barriers to entry, and respond to consumer demand.
I am often asked whether the U.S. military should prioritize high-volume, low-cost equipment or exquisite programs. Unfortunately, the answer is both. The United States and its allies still need exquisite aircraft, nuclear submarines, fifth-generation stealth fighters, and other high-end capabilities. But they should be optimized for specific use cases because they are too expensive to risk and too slow to replace in protracted conflicts.
The United States’ military operation in Venezuela in January, for instance, was stunningly complex and high risk, and it could never have been accomplished with cheap, mass-produced capabilities. Washington will always need such platforms, especially at the outset of a limited conflict, but they become less useful the longer the conflict lasts. Until one party’s will or ability to fight is broken, the battle lines are typically held through mass. Bespoke capabilities simply cannot win a major existential conflict. Mass and synchronized combat power remain the greatest deterrent, since an adversary is far less likely to start a war it believes it cannot sustain and win.
And yet the United States and its allies’ current defense architecture overemphasizes exquisite capabilities while their adversaries, namely China and Russia, possess vast industrial capacity to scale military production. Moreover, these adversaries, together with North Korea and Iran, place a fundamentally lower value on human life, which means that, in this new era of warfare, a protracted conflict plays to their strengths: they can sustain losses—in lives and treasure—that democratic governments cannot.
The entire Western defense ecosystem must be reformed from the ground up to avoid this fate and ensure it is structured for full-spectrum warfare. This ecosystem consists of three layers: a physical layer of critical precursors and infrastructure, a digital layer that enables free data flow, and an innovation layer that meets the future of warfare.
Regarding the first layer, the United States and its allies have let their physical foundation erode for decades. The U.S. Army alone has accumulated over $150 billion in unmet infrastructure needs, with many soldiers living in crumbling facilities and working on dated equipment. At the same time, it has offshored the critical raw materials necessary to build its most powerful systems and allowed manufacturing supply chains to wither. The U.S. military can’t close this gap quickly or efficiently on its own since federal budget processes are, by design, slow and inefficient with congressionally authorized projects generally taking years to even break ground.
Western militaries must instead think creatively to tap into latent resources and commercial expertise to close the infrastructure gaps that prevent industrial scaling. For instance, under Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s leadership, the U.S. Army stopped acting solely as a consumer of goods and began operating as a market incubator. By employing enhanced-use leases, it is trading land access to private industry in exchange for infrastructure investments. Mineral processing companies, for example, are building refinement centers on U.S. military bases to secure critical minerals and reshore supply chains. Similarly, the U.S. Department of Energy is bringing microreactors onto army bases for resilient, off-grid power supply, and hyperscalers are building on-base data centers with organic power generation to safeguard the compute necessary for AI-enabled command control and business enterprise functions. The most common structure has the private partners financing, building, and maintaining these facilities—at no upfront taxpayer cost—which frees the army to focus its resources and energy on other modernization efforts.
U.S. allies must pursue similar reforms. Protracted warfare necessitates secure, resilient infrastructure and supply chains to scale and synchronize military capability. Washington’s adversaries amassed industrial capacity and the materials to fuel it—the United States must continue to seize back its independent production capability.
The United States and its allies must also think creatively about digital compatibility. They must reverse decades of entrenched proprietary thinking across combat systems, factory floors, and everything in between. Over the past five years, the U.S. Army spent hundreds of millions of dollars attempting to connect hundreds of disparate systems. But it didn’t work, because of contractual limitations with many of the vendors and the sheer volume of human hours required to rewire decades of bad design. So in the first year of Trump’s second term, the army started jailbreaking them instead, which practically freed data that was previously held hostage in proprietary systems.
This allowed data to flow smoothly to any repository or system that was helpful for the army. The army connected hundreds of enterprise business systems that, among other things, allowed it to conduct the first personnel audit in over 50 years, saving an estimated $2 billion a year in redundant roles. The army also hosted the largest hackathon in history and, with the help of over 550 software developers, unlocked data transfer between more than 200 pieces of proprietary warfighting equipment. Systems that previously could not communicate—such as those demonstrated in Grafenwoehr—were integrated into a common operating picture in a matter of days.
If Western militaries can freely share data, the United States and its allies can overlay agentic AI models across the entire warfighting enterprise. Such tools can automate a wide range of operations, such as complex budgeting processes and create digital twins of the government-owned or government-operated manufacturing arsenals, maintenance depots, and ammunition plants. This will allow the most critical strategic manufacturers to run the same types of predictive supply chain analytics that are used in the private sector and provide an opportunity for allies to cross-load work across a connected manufacturing network. The collective alliance would become exponentially more productive and efficient, both on and off the battlefield. For future procurement, every military should enforce open-source standards to ensure that all capabilities can instantly communicate across digital networks.
Finally, the United States and its allies must reform the third layer of the defense ecosystem: the innovation timeline. Securing physical materials and open digital networks is useless if capabilities are fielded at the speed of bureaucracy. Western militaries must adopt commercial iteration and speed. Although they will likely always require bespoke capabilities such as tanks, helicopters, and rocket artillery that take years to field, they should mostly purchase commercially available technologies and services because it allows them to field capabilities in weeks, not years.
This so-called commercial-first approach will also help bridge the “valley of death” between prototyping and scaling that most defense innovations face. To further this cause, the U.S. Army last year established FUZE, a $750 million internal venture capital–like mechanism, to identify promising dual-use commercial technologies and provide funding to scale them. For compelling offerings, the U.S. Army quickly provides capital but then also transports winners directly to the field to test and iterate with soldiers. This is a huge innovation in itself since, in the past, programs like the Booker tank, the Commanche helicopter, and the Future Combat System spent years in development and cost billions of dollars—all before the military operators declared them failures. Now, the army has established a concierge booking platform that provides access within 30 days to domestic and international ranges where commercial developers can test and experiment side by side with soldiers. This model turns iterative failure and “failing fast” into a defining feature of innovation.
U.S. allies must similarly establish innovation engines that change the acquisition paradigm. The definition of success should not be exquisite capabilities that take decades to field but rather rapidly fielded solutions, preferably with commercial technology handed directly to deployed units who can test it and provide immediate, real-world feedback that refines the product. The United States and its allies must get private software developers in the mud with soldiers so that the innovation loop is as tight as possible.
With these reforms in place, the global defense ecosystem then needs a single, open marketplace where allied nations can transact as freely as any commercial market, without political barriers and bureaucratic friction. Domestic defense companies are currently isolated from one another because they survive in a monopsony: their government represents a majority of their sales, the company creates jobs and industry for its country, and it is therefore shielded from competition. But this stunts innovation, growth, and the competition that defines Western capitalist economies, particularly technology sectors. Introducing market forces to the Western defense ecosystem is the critical catalyst that will prepare the United States and its allies for the future of warfare.
The army recently launched marketplaces for its Unmanned Aircraft Systems and Counter-UAS. These began as a solution for domestic counterdrone interagency coordination, but they rapidly evolved into a more optimal model for achieving international military compatibility. Within months of their launch, the marketplaces had processed hundreds of millions of dollars in orders, and to date, over 25 allied countries have signed on to the programs. The marketplace will continue to expand to allow foreign vendors from allied nations to offer their products.
articles.summary: America and its allies must scale together for a new era of war.

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
DAVID SACKS is Fellow for Asia Studies at the Council on Foreign Relations and the author of the forthcoming book The Realist: Hans Morgenthau and the Purpose of American Power.
NICK SNYDER is Senior Fellow at the Hudson Institute. A retired U.S. Senior Foreign Service Officer, he served as Director of the State Department’s Office of Japanese Affairs from 2023 to 2025 and as Special Adviser to the Vice President for Asia and the Pacific from 2018 to 2020.
Japan, a country constitutionally bound to pacifism since World War II, is investing in its defense and contributing to regional security in ways that were previously unthinkable. Tokyo has nearly doubled its defense budget, purchased long-range missiles capable of striking military targets in China and North Korea, signed agreements that allow it to deploy its military overseas, stepped into combat roles in multilateral military exercises, and even lifted its prohibition on exporting weapons.
Japan’s current strategy benefits the United States. Tokyo is not moving away from its alliance with Washington or seeking strategic autonomy; instead, it is increasing the durability of U.S. power in the Indo-Pacific. The United States should be helping accelerate these reforms because a stronger Japan that is closely linked with other U.S. allies and partners in the region is essential to deterring a highly capable and assertive China. Japan is offering the United States a way to protect its vital interests in the Indo-Pacific at a much lower cost and with less risk than Washington would otherwise have to bear.
The United States, however, risks squandering this opportunity by not prioritizing its relationship with Japan. In November 2025, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi made comments about defending Taiwan that led Beijing to launch a massive coercion campaign against Tokyo, including throttling its supply of heavy rare-earth minerals and suspending Japanese seafood imports. Despite Takaichi’s statements being in line with U.S. policy preferences, Washington chose not to forcefully stand up for her in public. Then, in May 2026, Washington informed Tokyo that because of the war in Iran, it was delaying the delivery of Tomahawk missiles that Japan had purchased more than two years earlier, and in August, Washington temporarily moved the only aircraft carrier permanently deployed outside the United States from East Asia to the Middle East.
For now, Japan has looked past these developments and is still investing in its partnership with the United States. It does not have any better alternatives to Washington. But the U.S.-Japanese alliance will not automatically endure forever, and the current U.S. approach could soon drive Japan to lower its ambitions for the alliance. The U.S.-Japanese relationship is nearing an inflection point, where complacency in Washington about the alliance and dismissiveness toward Tokyo could leave the United States with less power and influence across the Indo-Pacific. The United States needs to visibly demonstrate its desire for a more ambitious U.S.-Japanese alliance and expand economic and military collaboration with Japan before it’s too late.
For decades, the U.S.-Japanese alliance rested on a division of labor: the United States guaranteed Japan’s security and Japan channeled its national energy into economic reconstruction. This bargain, although asymmetric, satisfied both parties. The United States got a secure regional presence to contain Soviet power in Asia during the Cold War while also preventing a revival of Japanese militarism, and Japan obtained the security it needed to rebuild its shattered economy.
But a cascade of external shocks in the past two decades forced Japanese leaders to revisit this postwar bargain. In 2010, when tensions flared over the disputed Senkaku Islands (known in China as the Diaoyu Islands), Beijing imposed an informal embargo on rare-earth mineral exports to Tokyo, showing its willingness to weaponize supply chains and highlighting Japan’s vulnerability to coercion. After U.S. President Barack Obama declared Syria’s use of chemical weapons to be a “redline” but did not enforce it, and as Washington did little to halt China’s militarization of islands and shoals in the South China Sea, Japan started to question the credibility of U.S. commitments. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, in 2022, further demonstrated that great powers were willing to use force to redraw territorial borders. And in the wake of U.S. Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s visit to Taiwan that same year, China’s aggressive live-fire military exercises made clear to Japan that a cross-strait conflict was no longer only a theoretical concern. Tokyo gradually concluded that it needed to invest in its own power and take more responsibility for protecting its interests.
Since 2016, Japan has pursued a strategy known as the “free and open Indo-Pacific,” which seeks to connect countries along the Indian and Pacific Oceans with a shared commitment to the rule of law, freedom of navigation, and free trade. As part of this strategy, Japan worked with the United States to revive the Quad—a partnership among Australia, India, Japan, and the United States—which has worked to improve the detection of illegal maritime activities and protect undersea cables. Since 2022, Japan has signed reciprocal access agreements with Australia, the Philippines, and the United Kingdom, allowing military personnel to train and operate in one another’s territory. These agreements laid the groundwork for further military cooperation. Earlier this year, Japan sent 1,400 troops to participate in combat roles for the first time in the annual U.S.-Philippine joint military exercises, where they fired a surface-to-ship missile from Philippine soil—another first in the postwar era. The possibility of revising Article 9 of Japan’s constitution, which renounces war and prohibits a traditional standing army, is no longer taboo in Tokyo.
Japan is also increasingly translating its industrial power into security partnerships. It is developing a sixth-generation fighter jet with Italy and the United Kingdom. In 2023, Japan launched an official security assistance program to provide military equipment and infrastructure to its partners, including giving coastal radar systems and patrol boats to the Philippines to help it track Chinese activity in the South China Sea. In 2026, Tokyo lifted its decades-long ban on exporting lethal arms and agreed to build three frigates for Australia and to jointly produce eight more.
Most significant, Japan has indicated that it is willing to play a more active role in U.S.-led efforts to deter a conflict over Taiwan. In November, Takaichi stated that a Chinese blockade of Taiwan could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan—a designation that would give Tokyo the legal authority to exercise collective self-defense and respond militarily. A solid majority of Japanese citizens supported Takaichi’s comments: they know that Japan cannot avoid such a conflict because Yonaguni, Japan’s westernmost island, is only 70 miles from Taiwan. That reality was brought home when Chinese missiles landed in Japan’s exclusive economic zone as part of the intimidation campaign Beijing launched after Pelosi’s 2022 visit to Taiwan.
To back up its rhetoric, Japan has upgraded its military infrastructure in the Ryukyu Islands, the territory closest to Taiwan. In 2024, Japan’s navy also transited the Taiwan Strait for the first time, and Tokyo procured 400 Tomahawk cruise missiles from the United States. In 2025, Japan established a permanent Joint Operations Command to unify its land, sea, air, and cyberspace domains under a single operational commander and to enable direct, real-time coordination with U.S. forces. By increasing its military might and complementing U.S. capabilities, Japan is aiming to preserve U.S. power in the region while deterring Chinese aggression.
The United States, however, has done little to publicly embrace Japan’s policy shift. It also has not taken steps that would calm a nervous region. In addition to delaying missile shipments to Tokyo and withdrawing its aircraft carrier from the region, the United States has scaled back or canceled joint military exercises with South Korea. It put a major arms sale to Taiwan on hold, and the war in Iran is likely to further delay the delivery of weapons that Taiwan has already purchased. At the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore, in May, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth omitted Taiwan from his remarks—the first time it had not appeared in such a speech in a decade—casting further doubt on the strength of U.S. commitments to Taipei. Some administration officials argue that Washington is merely trying to avoid unnecessarily infuriating Beijing. But rhetoric matters, especially since China wants to exploit signs of supposed American decline to make its rise to regional dominance appear inevitable.
Japan remains committed to its alliance with the United States and is still trying to strengthen it. But this should not breed complacency in Washington. Without sustained support from Washington, the U.S.-Japanese relationship will weaken, depriving the United States of its best partner in the world’s most consequential region. If U.S. President Donald Trump were to make major concessions to Beijing on Taiwan’s status, withdraw troops from South Korea, or refuse to defend the Philippines during a clash in the South China Sea, Japan would have no choice but to consider reorienting its foreign policy away from the United States.
An uncertain Tokyo would need to reassess many of its relationships, and it may seek closer ties with U.S. adversaries in ways that go against Washington’s interests. To reduce pressure on its northern flank and gain access to much-needed energy supplies, Japan would likely accommodate Russia by reducing support for Ukraine. Japan could also seek to improve its ties with the military junta in Myanmar to secure access to critical minerals and might even explore purchasing discounted Iranian oil. Most consequentially, without U.S. leadership, Japan could pull back its support for Taiwan, leaving the island vulnerable to Chinese aggression.
If Japan felt it could no longer rely on U.S. extended deterrence, it would likely seek to develop nuclear weapons of its own. After all, China, North Korea, and Russia all have large nuclear arsenals. Japan would feel compelled to make itself invulnerable to nuclear coercion. If Japan were to pursue nuclear arms, which it could do relatively quickly, South Korea would not be far behind, turning the region into a nuclear powder keg.
Japan would almost certainly embark on a massive conventional military build-up. China, assessing that Japan was exposed without U.S. protection but that its window to act might close as Japan increased its military power, would likely press its claims in the East China Sea, sharply increasing the risk of conflict. Without the United States acting as mediator, Japan’s cooperation with South Korea could also erode, leading Tokyo and Seoul to revert to their more traditionally antagonistic relationship.
If Japan also decided that it did not want to host as many U.S. forces, Washington would lose its best foothold in the region, diminishing its ability to project power in the Indo-Pacific and to ensure that vital markets remain open. Although the United States could base more forces on Guam or seek greater access in Australia, these are farther from places where conflict is likely to emerge—namely, Taiwan and the South China Sea—and would limit U.S. options for how to respond.
The United States should reward Japan’s faith in the alliance rather than ignore it. Washington can take steps to encourage Japan to continue in a strategic direction that benefits the United States, bolster deterrence at a time when doubts about U.S. commitments are growing, and send a powerful signal to China that its coercion of Japan will not succeed, in turn deterring Beijing from attempting to coerce other U.S. allies and partners. A strong U.S.-Japanese alliance will be critical to winning the long-term competition with China and securing U.S. interests in the Indo-Pacific, and Japan’s actions have made it easier for the United States to benefit from the relationship.
To start, the United States and Japan can work together to produce a wider array of cutting-edge weapons such as precision-guided missiles. This would simultaneously help Washington address its worrying shortages of critical munitions and provide a boost to Tokyo’s promising defense industrial base. U.S. and Japanese companies worked together to design and produce an antiballistic missile, and the two countries have also committed to pursue the joint production of U.S.-designed interceptors and advanced medium-range air-to-air missiles, weapons that are in short supply and are critical to a U.S.-led defense of Taiwan. In 2025, Japan exported to the United States interceptors it built under a licensing agreement; it could make more, but bottlenecks in U.S. supply chains for the necessary component parts have slowed production. The U.S. government can give Japanese companies licenses to manufacture more components domestically and to certify Japanese suppliers.
The United States and Japan can also more closely integrate the planning and execution of military operations, both to enhance deterrence and to enable more rapid decision-making if deterrence fails. They can start by making fuller use of Japan’s southwestern islands as a base of operations. U.S.-Japanese deployments in the Ryukyu Islands, which lie off Taiwan’s northeastern coast, complement U.S.-Philippine efforts in the Bashi Channel, the waterway to Taiwan’s south, creating the ability to deny Chinese maritime dominance on both flanks of Taiwan. The United States and Japan should establish a rotational U.S. military presence in Ishigaki, a major outpost in the Ryukyu Islands, where Japan’s Ground Self-Defense Force already has a camp equipped with a mobile antiship cruise missile unit.
Japan’s investment in its intelligence apparatus has made possible greater cooperation with the United States, too. In the past, intelligence sharing lagged behind other forms of U.S.-Japanese cooperation because Tokyo lacked a centralized intelligence agency and because its security clearance regime and cybersecurity practices did not meet U.S. standards. But in 2026, Japan established a National Intelligence Council and a National Intelligence Bureau, and it is working with U.S. firms to set up a top-secret cloud infrastructure, finally giving both parties greater confidence in sharing sensitive information. The United States can now create a viable path for Japan to join the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing partnership, which would enable it to receive more sensitive intelligence and pave the way for even closer U.S.-Japan operational planning.
U.S.-Japanese economic cooperation can also help both sides overcome weak points in their supply chains. China’s dominance of critical minerals and rare earths is a major vulnerability for both Washington and Tokyo. The two countries’ development finance institutions should establish a joint critical minerals fund to coinvest in mining, refining, and magnet-manufacturing capacity, which would accelerate both states’ efforts to eliminate their dependence on China. Energy cooperation can also be mutually beneficial: the United States is now the world’s largest natural gas exporter, and Japan has world-class import terminals, storage, and gasification infrastructure to turn liquefied natural gas into usable energy. Making Japan the transshipment and distribution hub for U.S. LNG into South Korea, Taiwan, and Southeast Asia would increase energy security for U.S. allies and partners and build a larger market for a key U.S. export.
The mixed signals that Washington is sending about the future of its alliance with Japan have raised questions throughout Asia about the future of U.S. power in the region. One way to allay fears that the United States is retrenching from the world’s most important region is to chart an ambitious course for its most critical alliance. For now, Japan has staked its future on the United States, but its continued course depends on the United States also choosing to loudly and publicly embrace Japan. Washington has a rare chance to elevate a critical alliance to new heights. If the United States allows the alliance to atrophy, however, Washington, Tokyo, and the region alike will suffer.

articles.title: The Coming Taiwan Crisis
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
JONATHAN A. CZIN is Michael H. Armacost Chair in Foreign Policy Studies at the Brookings Institution’s China Center and a co-host of the podcast The Beijing Brief. He was Director for China at the National Security Council from 2021 to 2023 and previously served as a member of the Senior Analytic Service at the Central Intelligence Agency. The views expressed here are his own.
As U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping meet in Washington this week, the Taiwan Strait, the waterway that has long been a flash point between the two countries, has seemed remarkably quiet. Chinese fighter jets regularly cross the centerline between Taiwan and the mainland. Chinese warships maneuver to the east of the island. And Beijing uses its coast guard to continually harass ships in the area. Yet for nearly a year, Beijing has avoided the large-scale military exercises that had become a regular feature of its coercion of Taiwan after former U.S. Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s visit to the island, in 2022.
That shift stems in large part from renewed optimism in Beijing. Although the Trump administration has not formally changed its policy toward Taiwan, Trump’s statements after his prior meeting with Xi in May undermined Taipei’s confidence in the United States’ commitment to the island. “I’m not looking to have somebody go independent,” he said at the time. “And, you know, we’re supposed to travel 9,500 miles to fight a war. I’m not looking for that.”
For years, many in Washington and across the Asia-Pacific region assumed that 2027 would be the next potential pivot point for Beijing’s Taiwan policy, because Xi had directed the People’s Liberation Army to be prepared for a cross-strait military confrontation by that date. Yet as 2027 approaches, it appears exceedingly unlikely that Xi is gearing up to employ lethal force any time soon. Xi has been willing to conduct systematic purges of his military high command, in part because he is not worried about a cross-strait crisis in the near future. For now, Xi seems to feel confident that he can effectively manage both Washington and Taipei.
But Xi remains deadly serious about organizing his force for a conflict over Taiwan in the coming years. The next pivotal date will not be 2027, when Xi is expected to begin a fourth term, but 2028, when both the United States and Taiwan will hold presidential elections that will determine the future trajectory of the cross-strait dynamic. In all likelihood, Xi will find himself frustrated by the outcome of Taiwan’s next election, which will make the situation more fraught than it is now. The coming two years are thus a crucial window for Washington to work with Taipei to prepare for what will likely be a far more turbulent period in the Taiwan Strait after 2028.
Rather than let doubts about its support for Taipei deepen, Washington should lean into its relationship with the island. In many ways, Taiwan has refashioned itself into a model partner, both by reorienting its economy toward the United States and away from China and by boosting investments in its own defense. At the very least, Trump should approve the $14 billion arms package that is on his desk, even if that means dividing the sale into smaller tranches to avoid escalating tensions with Beijing.
China will not welcome a series of U.S. arms sales, but historically Beijing has shown far more concern for high-profile gestures of political support for Taiwan, such as Pelosi’s visit, than over the bureaucratic details of U.S. weapons transfers. And leaving arms sales in abeyance carries its own long-term costs. By forgoing this minimum step, the administration will be complicit in Beijing’s bid to establish a veto over U.S. arms sales and, by extension, over the cross-strait dynamic. After 2028, the diplomatic price of such support for Taipei is likely to rise, as an aging Xi may conclude that further delay on Taiwan no longer works in his favor.
Xi’s optimism is predicated on the hope that the opposition party, the Kuomintang, will regain power in 2028 after a dozen years of rule by the Democratic Progressive Party, which the mainland reviles as separatist. Beijing has had no visible engagement with the government since the DPP came to power in 2016—a marked departure from Xi’s approach to the previous administration. In 2015, Xi became the first Chinese leader since Mao Zedong to shake hands with his Taiwanese counterpart, a precedent he must have relished. Yet rather than becoming part and parcel of what Xi and his propagandists call the “new era” for China under his rule, Taiwan has steadily drifted away from the mainland, frustrating his ambitions to begin the political process of annexing the island. Annexation, not a costly and likely catastrophic military invasion, is his ultimate goal.
Xi’s hopes rose in November 2025, when Cheng Li-wun unexpectedly became chair of the Kuomintang. Cheng has advocated a much softer line toward China, emphasizing the common Chineseness of citizens on both sides of the strait and the need for cross-strait dialogue. In April 2026, she traveled to Beijing to meet with Xi just weeks before he hosted Trump. The meeting positioned Xi to depict his Taiwan policy as conciliatory and reasonable, despite his hard-line approach to the ruling party over the past decade. His willingness to receive Cheng signals that she has become the linchpin of his hopes for advancing discussions about Taiwan’s status after 2028. Yet hope is not a strategy, and Cheng’s prospects even for becoming the KMT’s candidate in 2028, let alone for prevailing in the general election, are precarious. Her pro-Beijing views are not widely shared even within her own party. Cheng was a dark-horse candidate who secured the position of the KMT chair with just over 50 percent of the votes, and only 27 percent of the population supports her party.
That means that in 2028, Xi will likely confront either a fourth consecutive DPP administration under current President Lai Ching-te or a more moderate KMT leader who is warier than Cheng of Xi’s embrace. Should Lai secure a second term along with a renewed majority in Taiwan’s Legislative Yuan, it would devastate Xi’s hope that the KMT offers a viable alternative. After Lai’s victory in the 2024 election, Beijing consoled itself with the fact that he prevailed with just a plurality of the vote and lost control of the legislature to the KMT; it spun the result as a sign that most of Taiwan’s voters did not support Lai’s approach to the mainland. That was not just propaganda but a genuine rationalization for the manifest failure of Beijing’s cross-strait policies. Those shortcomings will be harder to explain away in 2028, especially if voters treat another Lai victory as a rebuke of the KMT’s more conciliatory posture. Xi at that point would be the steward of a stagnant Taiwan policy that has produced no political progress over more than a dozen years.
Xi’s looming dilemma underscores the hollowness of the Chinese Communist Party’s Taiwan strategy. His predecessor, Hu Jintao, tried a softer approach toward the KMT administration of Ma Ying-jeou, but the effort backfired. In 2014, young protesters in the Sunflower Movement occupied Taiwan’s legislature amid widespread opposition to a trade deal meant to deepen cross-strait integration. When the DPP took power in 2016, Xi—who had already demonstrated his comfort with a more muscular national security policy—shifted to coercion without diplomacy, cutting off all visible channels of communication with Taiwan’s political leadership. The goal has been to convince the people of Taiwan that the status quo is unsustainable, that annexation is inevitable, and that they should therefore acquiesce to Beijing’s overtures.
Xi is likely to be more impatient about resolving the Taiwan issue in his fourth term; by the end of it, he will be nearly 80. Although he may now feel that time is on his side, he is less likely to feel that way then. And especially if he is frustrated by Taiwan’s 2028 election outcome, he may be tempted to reach for more coercive actions. Xi likely learned from the Pelosi kerfuffle that he can go quite far in threatening the island: China’s over-the-top response in 2022 included firing missiles over Taiwan for the first time since the Taiwan Strait crisis of the 1990s, as well as imposing maritime exclusion zones around the island. Yet it did not provoke a full-blown crisis with the United States or cause tangible repercussions for China. Xi may also have more confidence in his high command after the 21st Party Congress, next year, when he will reshuffle his leadership team. He will presumably finish replacing the dozens of senior officers he has purged during his third term and may reorganize the military’s top ranks altogether.
But Xi would have to go beyond his 2022 response to make Taipei and Washington heed his grievances. This might include a more sustained, punitive, and risky military pressure campaign, even if no shots were fired, such as stopping foreign ships at sea, declaring multiple zones near Taiwan off-limits to international maritime traffic, and seeking to disrupt high-profile U.S. arms deliveries on commercial carriers. That would fall short of the full-blown blockade or quarantine that many in Washington have long feared, but it would send the message that Taiwan remains connected to the outside world only with Beijing’s acquiescence.
Yet in any such scenario, the off-ramp and the endgame are unclear. A Chinese decision to escalate might push Taiwan’s voters toward grudging acceptance of rule by the mainland—but it might just as easily backfire, creating a rally-around-the-flag effect on the island and augmenting anti-Beijing sentiment. That is what happened in the wake of the third Taiwan Strait crisis, in the 1990s, when Beijing’s threats against the DPP before the 2000 election helped the party win its first presidential race.
Xi could, of course, go for a full blockade or quarantine, or even seize one of the islands that Taiwan governs that sit alarmingly close to the mainland. Yet over 14 years in office he has shown that he is neither impulsive nor especially violent in his conduct of foreign policy, preferring steady, incremental pressure over a single decisive blow. Those riskier options could very well fail, undermining the premise that has animated him for decades: to secure his legacy as the leader who set Taiwan on the path toward what Beijing calls “reunification.” A quarantine or blockade would also play in some ways to the strengths of the United States in a crisis, allowing it time to muster a coalition of the willing to impose costs on Beijing.
These more violent options could become more tempting for Xi if a so-called restrainer who is suspicious of traditional U.S. partnerships enters the White House after the 2028 U.S. election. Such a president might be skeptical of U.S. interests in Taiwan, or of reinvigorating the alliances and partnerships that the United States would need to marshal to protect it. Even if a more conventional candidate prevails in 2028, China will likely have learned a great deal from the current war in Iran about the limits of U.S. power and Washington’s political and material ability to persevere. Key U.S. munitions stocks will take years to rebuild, and the conflict with Iran has exposed the vulnerability of U.S. overseas bases and naval logistics. Those problems will persist into the next administration, constraining the ability of the United States to respond to China in a crisis, regardless of what U.S. policymakers might want to do.
In the meantime, the United States and Taiwan have an opportunity to toughen up the island while Xi waits to see what the 2028 elections bring. Under the DPP, Taiwan has ended years of complacency about the threat from the mainland. It has stepped up investment in its own defense and pivoted its economy away from China more than almost any other state, including the United States. It has also demonstrated the will, the wherewithal, and now an incipient capacity to confront the challenge before it.
Most notably, after years of procuring U.S. weapons systems that would be useless in a conflict with China, Taiwan has finally gotten serious about defense reform. In May, it passed a supplemental bill appropriating $25 billion for the military. One of the central challenges facing that military now is not just how to acquire new capabilities but how to integrate them into the force. Indeed, the most contested political issue on Taiwan this year was defense reform, particularly appropriations for expanding the domestic drone industry. The KMT held up the legislation before acquiescing ahead of the island’s midterm elections, which will take place in November. Yet the mere fact that this is what the parties are fighting over is itself a hopeful sign of the government’s concern about defense.
The program for toughening Taiwan is not limited to the military. The government is serious about the trickier task of enhancing “whole-of-society resilience,” a delicate balancing act of acclimating the public to the threat from the mainland—and the possibility that it might one day invade or blockade the island—without inducing panic or resignation. Taiwan’s private sector shares many of the same temptations as firms around the world to buy cheaper Chinese goods, but the government is intent on keeping “red” components out of supply chains for government procurement.
Meanwhile, Taiwan’s economy is growing at a breathtaking rate, which means that it will have the fiscal space to fund military modernization in the coming years. It also has become far less dependent on China economically. Whereas in 2010 more than 80 percent of Taiwan’s outbound investment went to China, today less than ten percent does. Taiwan’s growth is instead fueled by its world-class semiconductor industry, which has capitalized on the AI boom. With a population of only 23 million, Taiwan has catapulted to become the fourth-largest trading partner of the United States. And it is not just selling its wares there: its leading companies have promised to invest hundreds of billions of dollars in the U.S. economy. In February, Taiwan became one of the first states to finalize a trade deal with the Trump administration. Unlike most U.S. trade partners, Taiwan seems genuinely pleased with the outcome, because it narrows the gap between the tariff rate on Taiwan’s goods and the rates on goods from its regional competitors Japan and South Korea.
Unfortunately, rather than capitalizing on these deepening economic ties and on Taipei’s serious approach to defense, Washington is undermining them. The structural forces all favor a closer relationship, but the diplomacy—which should be the easiest part of getting this right—has become the weakest pillar. Trump’s May visit to Beijing stoked anxiety in Taipei that he would sell out the island’s interests with a grand gesture. Instead, the president was at pains to stay on message for most of the trip, only to fumble in the comfortable setting of a Fox News interview. Trump described arms sales as a bargaining chip he could use with Beijing, unsettling decades of precedent whereby American presidents refused to consult Chinese leaders on the subject. In the days and weeks afterward, top U.S. officials emphasized that policy toward Taiwan had not changed, but the damage had been done.
More seasoned observers of U.S. policy on Taiwan were rattled less by the president’s rhetoric than by his actions, particularly his hesitation in moving forward on the $14 billion arms package. As a practical matter, the deficiencies of the U.S. defense industrial base and procurement process mean that the capabilities in that package would not arrive in Taiwan before the end of Trump’s term, which explains his lack of enthusiasm for it. And even once the materiel arrives, Taiwan will need time to assimilate its capabilities into its force so that it can employ them effectively.
But the long lead times only underscore the need for the administration to make haste now, when it has a willing partner in Taiwan with the fiscal space to make these purchases, and when Xi is waiting to see what 2028 will bring. The next administration may not have such a good opportunity to enhance Taiwan’s self-defense capabilities, and Taiwan will need all the capacity it can muster to deal with an aging and potentially more cantankerous Xi.
If the KMT wins in 2028, it may also lack the DPP’s enthusiasm for defense cooperation with Washington. Meanwhile, Xi is in the midst of a painful renovation of his military high command, which, when finished, could change the calculus in its own way. Thus, the fragile gentleman’s agreement between Trump and Xi could afford the diplomatic space to take advantage of this window without precipitating a crisis.

articles.title: How Iran Changed War
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
MICHAEL C. HOROWITZ is Senior Fellow for Technology and Innovation at the Council on Foreign Relations and Richard Perry Professor and Director of the Perry World House at the University of Pennsylvania. From 2022 to 2024, he served as U.S. Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Force Development and Emerging Capabilities.
When the United States began bombing Iran, it expected to quickly overwhelm the country’s government. In the war’s first 24 hours, American and Israeli forces hit roughly 1,000 targets. Over the following 37 days, they blew up 12,000 more, laying waste to much of Iran’s military infrastructure. The strikes killed Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, Iran’s minister of defense, and the head of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
But more than six months later, the Iranian regime not only remains intact; it is perhaps stronger than before. It immediately replaced lost officials and struck back at Washington and its regional partners. And it shuttered the Strait of Hormuz, driving up energy prices around the world and winning newfound political leverage—all to the great frustration of U.S. officials.
There are several reasons why Iran performed surprisingly well. For one, the country had long planned for American and Israeli attacks, so it was prepared to reconstitute its government when top leaders were killed. It was also able to import enough goods to keep its economy from completely collapsing despite a U.S. naval blockade. But one of the most significant factors is that the Islamic Republic had built up a large arsenal of cheap yet accurate drones and missiles. These munitions made Iran’s counterattacks effective and allowed it to close the strait—and thus deter American escalation.
In doing so, Iran has demonstrated something broader. The age of what I called precise mass—or high-volume, low-cost, precision-guided weapons—is well underway. It is no longer possible for the U.S. military, or any military, to win a full-blown war simply by using small numbers of exquisite weapons to dazzle opponents. Weaker countries can match stronger ones through offensive barrages. Offense is currently cheaper than defense: the price of effective interceptors has yet to fall to the level of attack drones and missiles, which means defending against precise mass is extremely costly. After all, militaries cannot endlessly block salvos of $35,000 Shahed-136 attack drones with $4 million Patriot missiles.
To be sure, the war in Iran also shows that advanced technology remains essential. The United States, for example, had great success hitting valuable Iranian sites because it has artificial intelligence systems that can identify and recommend targets faster than ever before. American exquisite weapons are still much harder to stop than cheaper ones, and they are more likely to destroy targets in a single strike. But the world is learning from Iran, building on what Ukraine had already made clear: the future of war lies in part in precise mass. Everyone will now embrace the imperative of producing and using hosts of cheap and disposable weapons systems, changing warfare and the military balance.
In war, it might seem as if wealthy states always benefit from new military capabilities. But the reality is more complicated. If a new system is expensive, it indeed favors rich incumbents. But if it is cheap and demands large organizational changes to adopt, other countries can take advantage just as quickly—if not faster. In fact, the most powerful militaries in the world often struggle in the face of required disruptive organizational change, as their prior success has created bureaucracies and organizational biases that make adoption harder. As a result, they have a hard time integrating new capabilities that cannot be plugged into their existing structures.
Precise mass is just such a capability. The most conventionally powerful militaries are organized around small numbers of exquisite, expensive, hard-to-produce weapons and platforms such as Tomahawk missiles and F-35s. Their units train and plan around these systems. They thus cannot easily adjust to precise mass capabilities, which require different kinds of training and entirely new conceptions of how to fight. Exquisite systems, for instance, are scarce, so units must take great care not to waste systems and to minimize the risk of destruction. With precise mass, by contrast, units are supposed to move quickly and not make the perfect the enemy of the good. This helps explain why the United States has struggled to adapt to precise mass—even though the country invented precision guidance and boasts the best military in the world.
Iran, meanwhile, has been broadly locked out of some more advanced military capabilities. As a result, it had to invest heavily in long-range, one-way attack systems and cheap ballistic missiles. The result is a war in which Iran has dramatically outperformed expectations. Tehran could not go blow for blow with the U.S. military’s exquisite weapons, but it did not need to, because it could rapidly fire relatively accurate drones and cheap missiles at U.S. bases and the region’s critical infrastructure. The United States has dealt billions of dollars of damage to Iran in turn, but only by burning through its stockpiles of Tomahawks, SM-6 missiles, and other expensive systems. As a result, Washington now has to sprint to resupply its own stocks and those of partners elsewhere, such as Taiwan and Ukraine.
Thanks to rigorous preparations, meanwhile, Tehran has been able to withstand the extensive damage. In the years before the war, Iran built a vast underground network of missile infrastructure spread across its territory that has proved impossible for U.S. and Israeli forces to eliminate thus far. The United States had even more trouble destroying Iran’s heavily dispersed missile production facilities, inverting assumptions that have guided American airpower campaigns since Operation Desert Storm against Iraq in 1991, where the emphasis was destroying existing weapons stockpiles.
Iran has shown that weaker states are no longer priced out of the military power game, and the United States has discovered that stronger states are not guaranteed the upper hand in major battles. Little wonder, then, that countries rich and poor are investing in precise mass. North Korea, for example, has received Iran’s Shahed technology and production equipment from Russia and is using it to develop its own cheap uncrewed vehicles. A company in Nigeria has contracted with a Turkish manufacturer to build 100,000 one-way attack drones at local assembly facilities. Poland has increased spending on drones and counterdrone systems from about $27 million in late 2023 to roughly $6.9 billion this year and established domestic drone factories. Six European states, including France, Germany, and the United Kingdom, signed a letter of intent to jointly develop a one-way attack drone with a range of over 300 miles and a target cost of less than $100,000. Saudi Arabia has unveiled its own attack drone modeled on the Shahed with a supposed range of more than 900 miles. And Japan’s governing party has requested a record $55.6 billion defense budget, largely so that it can buy great quantities of attack drones.
The Iran war shows that nearly every military can acquire lots of precision strike weapons that cost tens of thousands of dollars apiece. But defense remains much more expensive. There are very few reliable interceptors that cost less than $1 million. To repel Iran’s precise mass, Washington had to use about 65 percent of its Patriot interceptors and 35 percent of its THAAD interceptors, leaving it with roughly 1,000 and 250 of each type, respectively. The country’s partners in the Middle East are also running out of air defenses.
For the United States, this challenge was inevitable. The exclusive focus on exquisite systems since the end of the Cold War extended to how it approached defense, emphasizing antimissile systems intended to stop high-end ballistic and cruise missile attacks.
